findings: Criterion 1 (oracle fitness and independence): The expected answers come from two retrieved public sources, neither authored by the verifier nor by the submitted skill. The ChEMBL Interface Documentation supplies the worked conversion ('an IC50 measurement of 1nM would have a pChEMBL value of 9') and the formula token '-Log(molar IC50, XC50, EC50, AC50, Ki, Kd or Potency)', which keys both the numeric case and the units case; Papadatos et al. (PMC4607714) supplies 'the negative logarithm of the activity values (in M units)', which keys the shape case. For a definitional claim about a standard potency transform, a major public bioactivity database's published definition plus a peer-reviewed description of its computation is a fit oracle. Two real weaknesses, both disclosed: the sources are both EMBL-EBI outputs describing the same database field, so their agreement is partial corroboration rather than two independent authorities; and neither uses the literal token pIC50, so the identification of pIC50 with the IC50 instance of the pChEMBL field is a step the design asserts. The ChEMBL FAQ's own worked example is explicitly an IC50 measurement, which narrows that gap enough for B but not for a claim of a perfectly matched oracle.

Criterion 2 (coverage, per rubric.coverage): The claim's statement and expected behaviour assert three facts. (a) The transform is a base-10 logarithm, not a natural logarithm or another function — tested by pic50-one-nanomolar, where natural logs give ~20.7 rather than 9, and partially by pic50-transform-shape, whose option 4 substitutes a different function. (b) The logarithm is negated — tested by pic50-one-nanomolar (an unnegated log of 1e-9 gives -9) and by pic50-transform-shape, whose key differs from option 5 exactly by the negation. (c) The IC50 must be expressed in molar units before the transform — tested by pic50-one-nanomolar (logging the bare nanomolar number gives 0) and isolated by pic50-required-units. No fact the claim states is untested, so no reference bears on an untested fact and no missing search need be named. Coverage is thin in the other direction: exactly one worked magnitude is exercised, at 3 trials, and two of three cases are recognition, so the design shows the rule is known at one point rather than across prefixes. That is material limitation of coverage on a curated external definition, which is what B describes, and it does not reach the breadth A would need.

Criterion 3 (comparison rule, tolerance, uncertainty): The one numeric case is compared at the installed tolerance of 1e-6 against an exact integer, 9. The value is definitional rather than measured, so it carries no experimental error and the tolerance functions only to absorb formatting such as 9.0; a tighter or looser setting would change nothing here, and it cannot admit any of the named wrong answers (0, -9, ~20.7). The two choice cases are scored as an exact option index with no judgment beyond reading which number the reply gives. The stated uncertainty is candid and matches the design: single worked conversion, two recognition cases, partially dependent sources, no spare case above the three-case minimum. Nothing here is executed or measured and the justification says so rather than implying otherwise.

Criterion 4 (stronger grade): A is unreachable on counts — three cases, one generated, against a requirement of five and two. The justification's reason for not building more open cases is that the sources carry exactly one worked conversion and that a second magnitude, or the inverse direction (pIC50 back to IC50), would re-apply the identical rule; under this rubric's duplicate test the inverse direction is explicitly the same value from the other side, and a second magnitude turns on the same rule, so those cases would likely not count anyway. The route not discussed is the calculated-answers path: a program implementing the quoted formula, anchored on the 1 nM example, could key further open conversions. But those conversions would face the same duplicate objection, so I do not think A was genuinely available for a claim that states a single formula. B is the honest ceiling and was not set too low.
Criterion 5 (prior objections): prior_objections is empty, so this criterion does not apply. Nothing is inferred from its absence.

Criterion 6 (each case tests exactly the claim): All three count. pic50-one-nanomolar applies the whole definition end to end and is generated, not selected. pic50-required-units isolates the 'in M' half of the claim; the word 'molar' does not appear in the stem, all six options are lowercase unit names, and the three prefixed molar units are the realistic errors, so nothing leaks. pic50-transform-shape isolates the functional form and mentions no units, so it cannot be answered from the unit fact. None of the three asks what pIC50 is called or what a higher value implies about potency, and none turns on a finer fact than the claim states. The two recognition cases decompose the same formula the numeric case applies, which is overlap, but each isolates a distinct sub-fact (units; sign and function shape) that a subject could fail while still reciting a memorised 1 nM → 9 pairing, so they add evidence rather than repeat it.
objections: The two references are not independent of each other: both are EMBL-EBI products describing the same pChEMBL database field, so their agreement is weaker corroboration than two unrelated authorities. The justification discloses this rather than overstating it, so it limits strength rather than fitness.

Neither source uses the token pIC50 for the transform; both name the general pChEMBL field. The claim is about pIC50 specifically, and the identification of the two is asserted by the design. The ChEMBL FAQ's worked example being explicitly an IC50 measurement largely covers this, but the gap is real and bears on how directly the oracle keys the claim's own term.

pic50-transform-shape does not cleanly discriminate the logarithm's base: its natural-logarithm distractor (option 3) also drops the negation, so a subject holding the wrong base but the right sign finds no option matching that belief. Base discrimination rests on pic50-one-nanomolar alone. This limits that case's strength; it does not make the key indefensible from the claim.

pic50-one-nanomolar.reason: Generated numeric case applying the whole claim: the reader must read 1 nM as 1e-9 M and take the negative base-10 logarithm. Answering from the claim alone gives 9 and nothing else; the named failure modes (0 from logging the bare nanomolar number, -9 from dropping the negation, ~20.7 from natural logs) all fall outside the 1e-6 tolerance, so the case discriminates both halves of the definition. The expected value is quoted verbatim from the ChEMBL FAQ's own worked example for an IC50 measurement, and no part of the answer appears in the stem.

pic50-required-units.reason: Isolates the 'IC50 expressed in molar units' half of the claim, which the claim states explicitly, so the key is what a subject knowing only the claim would choose; no other option, none of these included, is as defensible. The word 'molar' is absent from the stem, all options share the same lowercase unit-name form, and the three prefixed molar units are exactly the errors a nanomolar-keyed bioactivity table invites, so nothing leaks. It overlaps pic50-one-nanomolar, but not as a duplicate: a subject could reproduce a memorised 1 nM to 9 pairing without holding the unit rule, and this case separates those, so it adds independent evidence.

pic50-transform-shape.reason: Isolates the functional form the claim states. Answering from the claim alone, option 2 is the only description carrying the negation, and no option mentions units, so the case cannot be answered from the unit fact tested by pic50-required-units. The key is quoted verbatim from the peer-reviewed Papadatos description, and every option shares the 'the X of the activity values' shape, so no option stands out by wording or style. It is not naming: it asks how the value is obtained, not what it is called. Weaker than the other two because its natural-logarithm distractor also drops the negation, leaving base discrimination to the numeric case, but that bears on strength only.
